# Results

**Hardware:** Apple M4 (10 cores), 16 GB, macOS (Darwin 25.3). Loopback only.
**Build:** `cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`, no sanitizers. **fd limit:** 1,048,576.
**Generated by:** `bench/run.sh 3 3` → `bench/results.jsonl` → `bench/analyse.py`.
**Cache OFF (`-C 0`) for every I/O measurement**, asserted by `tests/phase5.sh` test 6.
Median of 3 runs, spread shown.

> **This benchmark was run twice.** The first attempt used `python3 -m http.server` as the origin
> and a single asyncio load generator; both saturated at ~2.4k req/s, *below* the proxy under test,
> so all three arms flatlined at the same number and the comparison was worthless. The origin is now
> a pre-baked-buffer server across 4 processes (`bench/fast_origin.py`) and the generator runs 4
> processes (`bench/multigen.py`). Calibration: **21,629 req/s** at 100 connections, ~2.5× the
> fastest proxy arm. See §6.

---

## 1. Concurrency sweep — the event loop LOSES, and that is the finding

| conns | thread-per-conn | thread pool (64) | event loop | origin direct |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 3,512 <sub>±51%</sub> | 2,320 <sub>±114%</sub> | 1,741 <sub>±75%</sub> | — |
| 100 | 8,592 <sub>±21%</sub> | **9,016** <sub>±12%</sub> | 3,025 <sub>±82%</sub> | 21,629 |
| 500 | **8,265** <sub>±12%</sub> | 8,043 <sub>±15%</sub> | 2,487 <sub>±94%</sub> | — |
| 1000 | **7,559** <sub>±10%</sub> | 6,460 <sub>±49%</sub> | 1,957 <sub>±9%</sub> | 14,701 |

p99 latency (ms):

| conns | thread-per-conn | thread pool (64) | event loop |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 2.7 | 4.7 | 50.5 |
| 100 | 11.5 | 13.2 | 67.9 |
| 500 | 159.1 | **131.4** | 332.3 |
| 1000 | 611.8 | **250.9** | 3,965.6 |

0 failed requests across the entire sweep.

**The event loop is 3–4× slower on throughput than either threaded backend at every concurrency
above 20, and its tail latency is worse.** That is the opposite of what `docs/phase6.md §3`
predicted, and it is not a measurement artefact. Two reasons, both structural:

**It uses one core out of ten.** A single-threaded event loop is a single thread. The threaded
backends spread the same work across the whole machine. Relaying 8 KB per request is not free — it
is `recv`, buffer append, `send`, repeated — so throughput here is bounded by one core's syscall
rate. This is why nginx runs **one event loop per core** with `SO_REUSEPORT` rather than one loop.
evproxy implements one loop, and pays for it.

**It makes two extra syscalls per state transition.** Every `want()` change costs an `EV_DELETE`
plus an `EV_ADD`, and a single request transitions through `ReadClient → WriteUpstream →
ReadUpstream → WriteClient → …` several times. The phase 4 epoch fix made that re-arm
*unconditional* — correct, because fd numbers get reused, but it removed the "same fd, same
direction, skip it" shortcut. Batching the kqueue changelist into one `kevent` call per loop
iteration would recover most of it. Not done.

**So the honest claim is narrower than "event loops are faster":** this event loop trades throughput
for connection density. Sections 2 and 3 are where it wins, and both are about *connections*, not
requests per second.

## 2. Memory per established connection

500 connections opened and held without sending anything.

| backend | idle conns held | RSS before | RSS with conns | KB per conn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| thread-per-conn | 500 | 1,488 KB | 9,600 KB | **16.22** |
| thread pool (64) | 500 | 2,560 KB | 2,560 KB | 0.00 |
| event loop | 500 | 1,504 KB | 1,824 KB | **0.64** |

Reproduced across all three benchmark runs.

**16.22 KB vs 0.64 KB per connection — ~25×.** A thread stack and its bookkeeping against a few
hundred bytes of connection state.

**The pool's 0.00 KB/conn is not a win — it is the ceiling in memory form.** With 64 workers, only
64 of those 500 connections were ever accepted into a worker. The other 436 cost nothing because
nothing was being done for them.

## 3. The ceiling — 64 slow clients, one per worker

| backend | slow clients | ordinary request | proxy CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| thread pool (64 workers) | 64 | **2.03 s** | **0.0 %** |
| event loop | 64 | **0.63 s** | 2.8 % |

Across three independent runs: the pool measured 2.15 s, 2.14 s, 2.03 s — consistently unable to
serve an ordinary request, at **0.0 % CPU** every time. The event loop measured 0.01 s, 0.01 s,
0.63 s.

**Nothing is busy.** 64 workers are each blocked on a slow client, holding a seat. This is the one
result no throughput benchmark can produce, because a throughput benchmark closes each connection
before opening the next — and it is why §1's throughput ranking does not settle the question on its
own.

Consistent with the small-scale versions: 4 slow requests took 2.18 s with 2 workers vs 1.09 s with
8 (phase 2); 16 slow requests took 8.68 s through a 2-worker pool vs 1.09 s through the event loop,
8.0× (phase 3).

## 4. The back-pressure result

| conns | thread-per-conn p99 | thread pool p99 | event loop p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 611.8 ms | **250.9 ms** | 3,965.6 ms |

The pool's bounded queue caps the tail. Under back-pressure it stops calling `accept`, so
connections wait in the kernel backlog instead of piling into the proxy. The unbounded arms admit
everything and pay at p99.

The same mechanism that produces the ceiling in §3 protects tail latency here. That is the actual
trade-off the pool makes, stated in both directions.

## 5. Cache lock contention — still not a result

| conns | thread pool (mutex) | event loop (no lock) | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 48 | 8,571 req/s | 9,213 req/s | +7.5 % |
| 248 | 8,955 req/s | 8,703 req/s | −2.8 % |

Earlier runs gave +9.5 % and −51.5 % at the same concurrency. **The sign is not stable, so no
conclusion is drawn.**

The architectural claim stands on the code and the startup log (`lock=mutex` vs `lock=none`) — the
threaded backends take a mutex on every cache lookup and the event loop takes none. What is *not*
established is that the difference is measurable at this scale. Given §1, any contention effect is
buried under the event loop's 3–4× single-core throughput deficit anyway.

## 6. Methodology, and what still limits it

**The origin has to be faster than the thing being benchmarked, or it *is* the thing being
benchmarked.** The first attempt violated this: the proxied arms measured *faster than the origin
they proxy*, which is impossible. Fixed by replacing `http.server` with a 4-process pre-baked
responder — the proxy's number rose from ~2.4k to ~9k req/s once the origin got out of the way.

**Ephemeral ports were not the constraint here**, contrary to the first attempt's diagnosis:
`TIME_WAIT` measured 0–7 sockets throughout, because the proxy and origin perform the active close
rather than the client. The 15 s settle was reduced to 3 s with no change in results.

**The concurrency-1 and -20 rows are unreliable** (±208–439 % spreads, occasional 2,018 ms stalls —
the SYN-retransmit signature) and are excluded from §1. They run immediately after the
1000-connection calibration. Measured separately with the machine settled, all three arms give
**~3,000 req/s at concurrency 1 with p99 under 1 ms** — no architectural difference, which is the
expected answer when there is nothing to multiplex.

**Still true regardless of re-runs:** one machine, loopback only, connection-per-request (the proxy
forces `Connection: close`, so every request pays a full TCP setup). Absolute req/s figures are not
capacity numbers.

## 7. What to trust

**Supported:**
- The event loop's throughput deficit (§1) — ~3–4×, low spread at 1000 connections (±9–10 %), with
  a mechanism that explains it.
- Memory per connection, ~25× (§2) — reproduced in all three runs.
- The pool's concurrency ceiling (§3) — reproduced three times, 0.0 % CPU every time.
- Back-pressure capping the tail (§4).
- All three backends behaviourally identical: 13/13 on `tests/phase1.sh` each, ASan+UBSan and TSan
  clean.

**Not supported:**
- Cache lock contention being measurable at this scale (§5).
- Any conclusion from concurrency 1–20 (§6).
- That a *well-implemented* event loop is 3–4× slower — one loop per core and a batched kqueue
  changelist would both narrow the gap. What is measured is this implementation.
